description: My name is Tomás Gonçalves, and I’m an Aerospace Engineering student at Instituto Superior Técnico. I’m deeply passionate about space exploration and driven to unveil mysteries. I’m targeting the Flame in Freefall challenge and I'm looking for highly motivated teammates If you want to push your limits, work as a dedicated team, and build a winning dashboard, let's connect!
summary:
Live app: https://spark-210503776654.us-central1.run.app/

Spark is a web dashboard that turns NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) combustion data into a clear answer to one question: which microgravity fire experiments were run in the atmosphere my crew will breathe? It places every test with known oxygen and pressure from 24 PSI combustion investigations on one map of oxygen concentration versus pressure. The user picks an atmosphere (the ISS cabin, a lunar base or custom values), reads the answer in plain sentences, and sees the investigations ranked by how closely their tests match it. Every number links to its NASA source. Spark agent, an AI helper running on Google Gemini, explains any part of the page in plain language, cites its sources and states what the data cannot show. Spark also surfaces gaps: in the PSI data, no solid material was tested inside the expected lunar habitat atmosphere, a finding computed from the data, not written by hand. Spark helps researchers, engineers and students find, compare and interpret fire-safety evidence in minutes.
details:
Live app: https://spark-210503776654.us-central1.run.app/

Slide Deck:

https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1PTamomx7nqr90yRylmMLXJIjlAJnl6U5TeMr0Iqz9wc/edit?usp=sharing

Fig.1 - Why fire is different in space: a teardrop flame on Earth, a sphere in orbit. Illustration, not data.

What it does. Spark compares NASA's microgravity combustion experiments with the atmosphere of a chosen habitat. The main view is an atmosphere map: one mark per test, plotted by oxygen concentration and pressure, with the expected lunar habitat zone (30% oxygen or more, 10.2 psi or less) shaded. The user picks the ISS cabin, a lunar base, a NASA test atmosphere or custom oxygen and pressure values. Spark answers first in plain sentences, then shows the evidence on demand.



Fig. 2 - The atmosphere map. Each mark is one real NASA test, plotted by oxygen and pressure. Twenty tests fall inside the lunar zone, all gas flames; no solid material was tested there.

It ranks the investigations by how closely their tests came to the chosen atmosphere, lists the nearest tests to any custom target, and states which kinds of material have no tests there. Each of the 24 investigations has its own page with its objective, fuels, test conditions, sensors, key results, publications and data-quality notes. Every number opens to its source: the NASA file and row, or the report page.


Fig. 3 - Investigations ranked by how closely their tests match the chosen atmosphere, with the fuel type in words.

What we found. Inside the lunar habitat zone there are 20 tests, all gas flames on a burner (PSI-159): 13 flames went out by themselves, 5 burned until the fuel flow was stopped, and 2 have no recorded result. A NASA report adds one burner test at 34% oxygen and 8.2 psi in which the flame burned steadily (PSI-20). No solid material, the fabrics and plastics a habitat is made of, was tested in this atmosphere in the PSI data. Every solid-material test ran near normal pressure, at 22.7% oxygen or less.

The AI agent. Spark agent explains any block in plain language, in four parts: what you are seeing, what it means for fire safety, what the data cannot show, and sources.


Fig. 4 - An experiment page with the Spark agent’s explanation: what you are seeing, what it means for fire safety, what the data cannot tell you, and sources.


The server builds the facts from the data files, and the model receives only those facts. Each explanation is checked before it is shown: every number and source ID must match the data, and claims that something will burn or is safe are blocked. If the check fails twice, the site shows a plain message instead of an unchecked answer. A chat panel, open from any page, answers follow-up questions using two server-side tools that query the test data, and shows each tool result with its source. All AI output is labelled as AI-generated.














Fig. 5 - The Spark agent chat answers follow-up questions from the NASA data and knows which view the user is looking at.



How the data was built. Each PSI investigation was turned into a structured record, and each experiment's test table was downloaded as published. A validator checks every record and reports problems instead of fixing them silently. Converters turn the tables into clean test points with units from their definitions. Rows with impossible values, duplicates and blank lines are excluded and listed with reasons. Burner-oxygen tests are kept apart from cabin-air tests.

Benefits and intended impact. PSI holds valuable data, but it is spread across many pages, tables and long reports. Spark lets a professor, student or engineer see in one view which evidence applies to a given habitat and, just as important, where evidence is missing. The central finding is a gap, which points to where experiments are needed before crews live at higher oxygen and lower pressure. As NASA publishes new results, such as SoFIE on the ISS and FM2 on the Moon, the same map can show whether the gap closes.

Creativity. Instead of listing investigations, Spark asks a concrete question, "was this tested in my atmosphere?", and answers it visually. It treats missing data as a result worth showing. It constrains the AI: the model explains verified facts and says what the data cannot show, rather than writing free text.

Factors we considered. Trust: every number links to a source, and AI text is checked and labelled. Honesty about limits: PSI has no partial-gravity data yet; 16 of the 24 investigations have no per-test oxygen and pressure, so they are listed but not plotted; the ranking weights are our own judgement and are labelled that way; experiments outside PSI are not shown as results; chat replies stream and cannot be checked before display; AI answers have not been reviewed by people. Scope: rocket and propellant fires are excluded, as the challenge states. Audience: plain enough for students, precise enough for researchers. Cost: a per-visitor limit on AI requests protects the service.

Tools. Backend: Python 3.12, FastAPI, Pydantic, Uvicorn. Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, assistant-ui, Tailwind CSS (chat panel only). AI: Google Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite on Vertex AI, through google-genai. Testing: pytest, Ruff and Vitest, about 990 automated tests run on every change. Deployment: Docker on Google Cloud Run. Data: 24 NASA PSI combustion investigations (19 flight, 5 ground), the Burning Rate Emulator final report, and NASA's "A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science".

Use of AI. Claude Code (Anthropic) wrote much of the code and documentation in small steps that we reviewed, with the full test suite run on every change. Claude (Anthropic) helped the team members produce the structured experiment records from the NASA sources, which we validated and spot-checked. We also used Claude for planning and reviewing options. Gemini powers the in-app Spark agent. The README states all of this.

The demo video was made with help from Claude, with an AI voice-over from ElevenLabs; the video carries a visible AI watermark.
